subtype: Approach: researching the person before writing [Thinking]
passage: In the university library in Toronto, Siddiq wanted to write to Amara, an engineer at a mapping company he admired. He almost typed "Hi, I'd love to work at your firm", then stopped and opened her profile instead. Her posts were mostly about routing delivery vans. Then he found a recorded talk she had given at a local meetup, about handling roads that closed suddenly. He watched it twice with headphones on and noted one thing she said: that real maps are always slightly wrong. His message became: "Your talk on road closures made me wonder how you decide when to trust old data. Would you have two minutes to point me to one thing to read?" He read it aloud once, and sent it.

qa.a: Amara's talk was about handling roads that closed suddenly.

qa.q: What is Siddiq feeling as he stops before sending the first draft?
qa.a: Siddiq feels cautious and thoughtful, realising that a generic line would waste her attention and choosing to prepare.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Siddiq add, and why?
qa.a: Siddiq could look for a mutual contact who could introduce him, because a warm introduction can make even a good message easier to answer.

qa.q: How might Amara see this message?
qa.a: Amara sees a question about her own talk and a small request, which shows the sender did real reading and makes a reply easier to write.

grounding: Shows researching a stranger's posts and talk before writing so that the message asks something specific and respectful.

subtype: Approach: researching the person before writing [Thinking]
passage:
In the college library's back corner, Jaya had a message box open and a blank line where the first sentence should be. The engineer she wanted to reach, Revati Menon, designed battery systems at the electric-scooter company Jaya dreamed of joining.
'Just say hi and ask for advice,' whispered Vinita from the next chair.
'Everyone says that. She must get fifty of those.' Jaya closed the message box and opened Revati's public posts instead. Mostly about cooling problems in batteries. Then a link: a twenty-minute talk at a conference in Chennai. Jaya put in one earphone and watched it through, taking notes.
'Okay,' she murmured at the end. 'She said the hardest part was testing in forty-degree heat. I can ask how they test in monsoon humidity. That's a real question, and it shows I listened.'
She wrote three lines. Vinita read them and raised her eyebrows. 'That sounds like someone she'd reply to.'

qa.q: How long was Revati's talk, and where was it given?
qa.a: It was a twenty-minute talk at a conference in Chennai.

qa.q: Why did Jaya close the message box, and what was she feeling?
qa.a: She felt uneasy that a plain 'hi' would be one of fifty, and wanted her message to be respectful and worth answering.

qa.q: What else could Jaya do if Revati does not reply?
qa.a: Send one short, polite follow-up after a week, and meanwhile find another engineer whose work she has actually studied.

qa.q: How might the message look to Revati?
qa.a: It stands out from generic requests because it asks about her own talk, which shows real interest and respect for her time.

grounding: Shows a student reading an engineer's posts and watching one of her talks before writing, so the message can ask something specific.

passage:
Hi Sahil,
You laughed at me for taking two days to send one message to that data engineer in Hyderabad. Here's why.
My first draft was 'Hello, I am a final-year student, please guide me.' Then I thought: if I got that from a stranger, what would I answer? Nothing, because there's nothing to answer.
So I read her public posts first. Most were about cleaning hospital records. Then I found a recorded talk she gave at a college fest, about how missing dates in patient files wrecked a whole model. I watched it twice.
My final message was four lines. It said I'd watched the talk, and asked one thing: how her team decides when to drop a record and when to fix it. She replied the next morning with a long answer and a link to a paper.
Two days well spent.
Divyansh

qa.q: What were most of the engineer's public posts about?
qa.a: Most were about cleaning hospital records.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel about the first draft after imagining receiving it?
qa.a: Divyansh felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, seeing that a stranger would have nothing in it to answer.

qa.q: What would you advise Divyansh to do after the engineer's reply?
qa.a: Thank her, read the paper, and come back later with one follow-up question that shows the answer was used.

qa.q: How might the engineer have felt reading the four-line message?
qa.a: She was likely pleased and felt respected, since the question came from her own talk, which made a long answer feel worthwhile.

grounding: Shows a student reading an engineer's posts and watching her talk before writing, so the message asks a specific, respectful question.
